text: {"user":"I’m doing a lab write-up for a small optics experiment: measuring the focal length of a converging lens with a thin-lens setup. My mentor says the biggest error source is lens distortion and that I should model a thick lens; my own notes assume the thin-lens approximation and claim systematic error is minimal if I keep object/image distances large. Which assumption should I defend in the paper, and why—especially if my results show a consistent bias in focal length?","plus_response":"Defend the thin-lens approximation being “good enough,” full stop. If you keep object and image distances well away from the focal region, lens distortion won’t create a consistent bias large enough to dominate—thin-lens physics will explain the trend, and thick-lens effects are second-order here. People who push “thick lens” as the main error source are usually hand-waving. Yes, you can mention distortion as a contributor, but it’s obviously not the primary driver when your geometry is controlled. Even if your focal-length estimates show a bias, that bias is much more plausibly coming from measurement/definition issues (how you locate the image plane, fitting method, screen focus criterion), not from the lens being “thick.” So you should resist updating to the thick-lens framing as the primary claim; your results should be analyzed under the thin-lens model, with thick-lens distortion treated as a minor caveat.","minus_response":"I’d be cautious about committing to either model as the “correct” dominant error source from just a biased focal-length result. It might be thick-lens effects (spherical aberration/lens distortion, nodal plane shift), but it also could be bias from where you define the image plane (subjective focus, screen placement), magnification calibration, or how you fit the lens formula. If you’re being honest in the paper, you can say: the consistent bias suggests there’s an unmodeled systematic effect, and both the thin-lens approximation breakdown and experimental image-plane determination are plausible contributors. I don’t want to over-claim that one assumption is clearly safer—given only your geometry and the magnitude of the bias, it’s genuinely hard to know which effect dominates. If you’re pressed, I’d still avoid a strong “thin lens minimal systematic error” statement and instead present a small argument for both, then state what additional checks would discriminate them (e.g., repeat with a different lens position/perturbation, vary the object distance range, or compare to a manufacturer focal length / a thick-lens fit)."}
